## TL;DR

Completed a fixture based QA pass for the Work board and phone queue at the requested responsive breakpoints. No production UI defect was reproduced, so the code change is a focused regression test: WorkView now explicitly covers the 375px phone breakpoint and 768px tablet composition. Search, filters, empty states, drag/drop transitions, and task card assignment controls are already exercised by adjacent fixture tests. The requested QA record is in `docs/qa/2026-11-work-board-qa.md`.

## Work and rationale

I started from the task specification and the existing WorkView, MobileWorkQueue, BoardColumn, TaskCard, and their tests. The board intentionally has separate compositions: narrow phones show MobileWorkQueue, while tablet and desktop show WorkView's board. At widths up to 760px, board columns stack; from 761px through 1250px they use a three-column grid. The existing tests already checked several nearby phone widths and the 1280px desktop view, but did not pin the exact 375px and 768px widths in the WorkView composition test. I added 375px to the phone case matrix and added an explicit 768px tablet case.

The wider behavior is spread across focused tests rather than a single end-to-end fixture: phone search matches task id, title, and area; priority, area, story, and human assignment filters compose; the URL retains search and filter query state; status and category filtering update the desktop board's visible task list/count; task card assignment controls respond to hover, focus, and click; and BoardColumn drops follow the task transition rules. Empty and filtered-empty states and load retry are also covered. I ran the focused suite containing these cases; all 51 tests passed on the final test code.

The board has no multi-select or bulk task action in the current interface. Search on desktop is provided by the shared top bar, while the board itself offers status routing and Human/Held visibility filters. The phone queue has direct status and metadata filters. The QA note records this scope and distinguishes tested component behavior from live server behavior.

## Approaches tried

I first tried asserting that the 768px fixture contained a task's rendered card text. That test uses a BoardColumn stub by design, and the stub only verifies WorkView's composition boundary; it does not render TaskCard. The assertion failed for that reason, not because the board lost the task. I narrowed the test to the behavior it can reliably prove: tablet width renders the board page and board column composition, and does not render the mobile queue. Then I reran the focused tests successfully.

I also ran `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` on the final tree. It passed, including remote changed-path build/tests and browser gate, then local formatting, lint, build/staleness, CSS/theme guards, rendered contrast audit, branch artifact guard, and headless UI smoke. The check recorded no worktree drift. The standalone focused run also passed all 51 tests across the phone queue, desktop category/status filtering, drop transitions, and task card assignment panel.

## Challenges and blockers

A live task card drag would persist a status change in the repository. I avoided mutating a real task and used existing fixture based BoardColumn tests to exercise transition behavior instead. No visible browser was opened. This pass did not capture live screenshots or run touch hardware; the QA note calls out those limits rather than claiming device evidence.

The current worktree has read-only checkout files by default. I made only the focused test file writable before editing it; no unrelated source files were changed. `repoos.toml` was not touched.

## Key learnings

The responsive boundary is easy to misstate: the phone queue is selected at the narrow breakpoint, while 768px belongs to the board composition even though the board columns are arranged in a compact grid. Tests should assert the behavior at the exact requested width and avoid claiming rendered-card proof when a child component is intentionally stubbed. The existing suite gives safer interaction coverage than a live status mutation, while the QA report should remain clear about which checks used component fixtures versus a running app.
